Zorba begins courting her, while the narrator notices a beautiful widow watched suspiciously by the local community. The partnership takes shape: the narrator supplies money and ideas, and Zorba supplies practical command and an appetite for experience.

Work begins at the mine, but dangerous conditions and poor prospects expose the weakness of the enterprise. Zorba throws himself into the labor and treats setbacks as problems for the body and imagination rather than occasions for retreat. He proposes a more ambitious plan: acquire timber from a monastery forest and build an aerial cable system to carry logs down the mountain. The narrator commits additional money, attracted as much by Zorba's confidence as by the economics. Their visit to the monastery introduces Zaharia, a tormented monk disgusted by the life around him. Back at the shore, Zorba's attachment to Madame Hortense deepens through a mixture of tenderness, performance, and desire. The narrator remains divided between observation and participation, especially in relation to the widow, while Zorba repeatedly urges him to stop translating every impulse into thought.

The cable project absorbs the partners' hopes. Zorba travels to Candia to buy equipment, leaving the narrator to manage without his energy. In the city he spends freely and becomes involved with a young woman named Lola; his letter reports the adventure with a frankness that angers and fascinates his employer. When he returns, practical work resumes, though the venture's finances are increasingly fragile. Madame Hortense has taken Zorba's courtship seriously and expects the security of marriage. Zorba avoids a direct commitment, and the narrator helps sustain assurances that neither man is ready to honor formally. Meanwhile the narrator's attraction to the widow becomes a test of the very lesson he thinks Zorba represents. He can describe freedom and desire more easily than act on them, and village scrutiny makes any approach to her dangerous as well as personally difficult.

Pavli, the son of the influential Mavrandoni, cannot bear the widow's rejection and takes his own life. The village converts grief into hostility toward her. The narrator nevertheless moves beyond his hesitation and finally becomes her lover, briefly experiencing the unmediated closeness that Zorba has pressed him to seek. Their night together does not free the widow from the community's judgment. Mavrandoni and other villagers regard her as responsible for Pavli's death, and a public confrontation forms around that accusation. Zorba recognizes the immediate physical danger and attempts to stand between the widow and the men pursuing her, while the narrator is forced to see how little private insight can control collective violence.

The widow is killed by villagers avenging Pavli despite Zorba's effort to save her. The narrator is left with grief and guilt rather than the liberation he had associated with acting on desire. Madame Hortense also declines rapidly from illness while clinging to the promised marriage and dies without the future she expected. Women from the village descend on her rooms and carry away her belongings almost at once. At the monastery, Zaharia acts on his hatred of the institution and sets it on fire. The partners press ahead with the timber scheme, now the last material hope of their Cretan undertaking. At its ceremonial opening, the cable apparatus fails catastrophically as the logs rush down, and the investment is destroyed in front of the assembled guests. Zorba and the narrator are left with no successful business and few illusions about the community around them.

With the mine and timber project ruined, the narrator and Zorba do not attempt to preserve appearances. They feast on what remains, drink, and dance together on the beach, turning the collapse into a final shared affirmation. A message brings news of Stavridaki's death, joining the narrator's Cretan losses to the friend whose departure framed his journey. The partners then separate: the narrator returns to his more reflective life, while Zorba resumes wandering, working, loving, and sending occasional letters from abroad. Years later a schoolmaster in Skopje informs the narrator that Zorba has died and had wished him to receive his santuri. The narrator does not go to claim the instrument. Instead, after repeated memories and dreams of his old companion, he accepts the need to set Zorba down in words. The account closes as an act of belated fidelity by the bookish observer to the man who taught him the claims of immediate life.
